On the Motion of the Heart, etc.

Since these things are so, it is evident that what I previously stated—that blood constantly passes through the heart—will also be confirmed. For we see in the physical state of the body that blood flows from the arteries into the veins, not from the veins into the arteries; we see, moreover, that almost the entire mass of blood can be drained from the arm itself, provided a proper ligature is applied, and that this is done with a single superficial vein opened by a lancet. Furthermore, we see it poured out so impetuously and in such abundance that it is clear that not only the blood contained in the arm below the ligature before the incision is quickly and briefly evacuated, but that the blood is drawn from the entire arm and the whole body, from both the arteries and the veins.
Wherefore, it must necessarily be confessed, in the first place, that blood is supplied by force and impetus, and is driven forward by force.

<summary>Harvey argues that blood flows from arteries into veins and confirms that the entire volume of the body's blood can be drained from a single limb through the force of circulation.</summary>
